results.title: Security and Accessibility Require New Statehouse Entryway
results.description: MONTPELIER — The Joint Legislative Management Committee has approved plans for the second phase of a new, more secure, and easily accessible entryway to the Vermont Statehouse. The entrance will be the single point of entry for all visitors during the legislative session and the ADA-compliant entrance year-round. In the upcoming session, legislators will be asked to continue funding the multi-year project. “This project is 100% about members of the public being able to safely visit their Statehouse,” Sergeant at Arms Agatha Kessler said in an interview with The Bridge. “It’s strictly about creating a safe, secure, and accessible entrance.” The post Security and Accessibility Require New Statehouse Entryway appeared first on The Bridge.

results.title: Gutting: the cost of chronic gut problems in NZ
results.description: Chronic gut problems, including irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), could be affecting 1 in 3 NZers and costing over $1.5 billion in healthcare costs per year. Unable to find any recent NZ data, and no data on Māori, researchers assumed chronic gut issues are as common in NZ as they are in Australia and the UK. Using a UK study that calculated the healthcare costs of each person with IBS, the researchers estimated how much chronic gut issues might be costing here. Until we get our own local data, the researchers say their 'crude estimates' should be understood as a likely underestimate of how common and costly chronic gut problems are.

results.title: NZ heart failure treatment not up to scratch
results.description: NZers with heart failure may not get the care recommended by medical guidelines, finds a new study. Researchers looked at a random sample of 328 heart failure patients' hospital records in the Auckland Region. Nearly half of them had a type of heart failure that should be treated with a combo of four drugs, according to guidelines, but less than 10% of them actually got all four treatments. This was because most of the patients weren’t eligible for a subsidy to pay for one of the drugs. The researchers say this initial study shows a considerable gap in care and they plan to create a nationwide registry to find out how heart failure is being treated across NZ.

results.title: Kyrgyzstan increases livestock breeding loans by 92% as output grows
results.description: Over the past five years, Kyrgyzstan has implemented a series of systemic measures to modernize its agricultural sector, focusing on livestock productivity, irrigation efficiency, and digital monitoring. According to the Ministry of Water Resources, Agriculture and Processing Industry, these initiatives combine direct financial subsidies with infrastructure development to reduce crop losses and improve land utility. Livestock and Breeding Credit To improve livestock breeds and overall productivity, the government introduced a preferential lending program with a 3% interest rate. The scale of this support has increased significantly: in 2025, 180 farmers received loans totaling 584.1 million soms. By October 30, 2026, the program expanded to 238 beneficiaries, with funding reaching 1.125 billion soms and a fund utilization rate of 91.3%. This financial injection contributed to an increase in the number of breeding farms from 186 in 2025 to 232. In the first nine months of 2026, the country saw growth in livestock output compared to the same period last year: egg production rose by 148.7 million units (22.6%), meat production increased by 12.6 thousand tons (3.9%), milk rose by 34.8 thousand tons (2.4%), and wool production grew by 64.4 tons (0.5%). Based on these results, the government plans to allocate 7 billion soms for livestock lending in 2027.
